item.title: Your Rational Mind Is a Myth, and 5 Other Hard Truths From The Laws of Human Nature
item.description: Robert Greene's The Laws of Human Nature uses Pericles, Howard Hughes, and Richard Nixon to show why almost none of us are as rational, self-aware, or immune to envy as we assume.
item.content:encoded:
Pericles ran Athens for over three decades by assuming everyone around him, including himself, was fundamentally irrational. He was right, and it’s the whole reason the city had a golden age under him and fell apart within a decade of his death.

That’s the opening case in Robert Greene’s The Laws of Human Nature, and it sets the tone for the whole book: humans like to believe we’re rational agents making reasoned choices, when in fact most of our decisions are emotional reactions dressed up afterward as logic. Greene spends 500-plus pages walking through the specific, recurring ways this plays out — in ourselves, in the people we trust, and in the groups we belong to — using historical figures as case studies instead of abstract theory.

Here are six of the sharpest ideas in it.

You think you’re rational. You’re not.

Pericles noticed something strange about Athenian politics: every leader around him believed he was acting rationally, had sound reasons for his decisions, and could always explain afterward why things went wrong. And yet the city lurched from crisis to crisis. The problem wasn’t a lack of intelligence — it was that intelligence was being deployed in service of emotion, not instead of it.

Pericles built his entire career around training himself out of this. He refused to make decisions while under the influence of a strong emotion, physically removing himself from heated debates until he calmed down. For decades it worked: Athens expanded its wealth, built the Parthenon, and avoided the needless wars other leaders kept pushing for. Then Pericles died of plague in the second year of the war with Sparta, and without him the city voted, within a few decades, to slaughter the men of a surrendered island and launch a catastrophic expedition against Syracuse that ended the Athenian empire for good. Same citizens, same institutions — just without the one man who’d trained himself to interrupt his own emotional reactions.

Share this: The test isn’t whether you feel rational — everyone does, including the people making terrible decisions. The test is whether you have a practice for catching yourself before you act on a strong emotion. Greene’s own suggestion: treat any decision made in a state of excitement, anger, or anxiety as provisional, and revisit it once the feeling has passed.

Judge people by their patterns, not their pitch

Howard Hughes inherited a profitable tool company, taught himself to fly, and built a public image as the ultimate self-made American maverick. He was also, demonstrably, a catastrophic manager — and the pattern was visible decades before his death. On Hell’s Angels, he fired three directors, ran up a budget of 3.8millionagainstrevenueofunder3.8 million against revenue of under 3.8millionagainstrevenueofunder2 million, and ended up directing it himself. On a WWII military contract to build reconnaissance planes, he burned through 6millionofa6 million of a 6millionofa9 million budget without delivering a single plane, and the Air Force canceled the order. In the 1960s, in almost the exact same sequence, he underbid the Army for a helicopter contract, failed to deliver on schedule, and lost $90 million trying to win the follow-on order.

Three different industries, three decades apart, same exact failure mode: hire someone competent, undermine their authority within weeks, insist on approving every detail personally, watch the project collapse. People who worked with him kept getting fooled by the same things — his charm, his technical fluency, his reputation — because they judged him by his résumé and his pitch instead of by what he had actually done the last three times.

Share this: Before trusting someone with something important — a job, a partnership, your money — look at what they did the last two or three times they were in a similar position, not what they say they’ll do this time. Greene’s line for it: character is destiny, and nobody does something just once.

Everyone has a Shadow, including the nice ones

Richard Nixon spent his public life cultivating an image of himself — “RN,” he called it in his notebooks — as a statesman in the mold of Lincoln, driven by his Quaker mother’s ideals. Privately, late at night with his staff, he returned obsessively to old grievances: the 1960 election he narrowly lost, the East Coast elites who’d snubbed him for attending Whittier instead of Harvard, the journalists he was convinced were out to destroy him. That repressed resentment didn’t disappear because he’d built a nicer public persona over it — it came out sideways, in a secret White House taping system and, eventually, in Watergate.

Greene calls this repressed, denied part of the personality the Shadow, borrowing the term from Carl Jung. The more polished and consistently “nice” someone’s public front is, the thicker their Shadow tends to be — not because niceness is fake, but because something has to be done with the aggression, insecurity, and resentment every person actually has.

Share this: The people easiest to misjudge aren’t the openly difficult ones — they’re the ones whose public persona never cracks at all. Watch for the moments when someone’s voice or face changes for a split second under pressure; that’s the Shadow leaking through, and it tells you more than months of pleasant interactions do.

That envy you’re denying is running your social media feed

Studies cited in the book have found that even monkeys experience envy — it’s that deeply wired into social animals. Yet almost nobody will admit to feeling it; we experience the initial pang and almost instantly convert it into something more acceptable, like irritation or moral disapproval of the person who has what we want. Greene points to Robert Rubin, Goldman Sachs co-head and later U.S. Treasury Secretary, as someone who understood this instinctively: in meetings where he was clearly the most knowledgeable person in the room, he made a habit of asking junior staff for their opinions first and listening as if he meant it. Colleagues described him as nearly impossible to resent, in an industry built on resentment.

The book also makes a point that reads differently now than it might have before social media was the dominant way people compare their lives: a feed is a highly curated highlight reel, and constant exposure to other people’s best moments manufactures low-grade envy on a scale humans never had to process before.

Share this: When you notice the specific flash of irritation at someone else’s good news, don’t suppress it — name it as envy and ask what it’s telling you about what you actually want. Then do the less natural thing: try to feel genuine pleasure at their success instead of resentment. Nietzsche had a word for this, Mitfreude — joying with — and the book argues it’s rare enough that practicing it actively builds trust other people can feel.

Groups turn you into someone you wouldn’t recognize alone

In 1966, a studious teenager named Gao Jianhua was attending one of China’s most prestigious schools, dreaming of becoming a writer. Within months, as the Cultural Revolution swept through, he was patrolling the campus as a Red Guard while teachers he liked and respected were forced into “struggle meetings,” paraded in dunce caps, and in at least one case, driven to suicide. Jianhua didn’t start out as someone capable of any of this. Neither did most of his classmates. What changed was that they were operating inside a group dynamic that rewarded escalating zealotry and punished hesitation — and normal, previously decent people adjusted their behavior accordingly, in real time, without fully registering what was happening to them.

Greene’s point isn’t that this was a uniquely Chinese or uniquely political phenomenon. It’s that groups reliably pull individuals toward more primitive, more conformist, more emotionally reactive versions of themselves — in offices and online communities as much as in revolutions, just with lower stakes.

Share this: When you notice yourself adopting a group’s intensity about something faster than you’d normally form an opinion on your own, that’s the signal to slow down, not speed up. Ask whether you’d hold the same position if you encountered the facts alone, with nobody watching.

Thinking about death more often is the fix, not the problem

Flannery O’Connor was twenty-five when a doctor finally told her the truth her mother had been concealing: she had the same lupus that had killed her father at forty-five. Rather than retreating, she described the diagnosis as a second “bullet in the side” and moved home to her family’s farm to write with total focus, producing Wise Blood and the short stories that made her one of the sharpest American writers of her era, almost entirely under the shadow of a disease she knew would likely kill her young. It did, in 1964, when she was thirty-nine.

Greene uses her, along with Fyodor Dostoyevsky’s account of standing in front of a firing squad before a last-second reprieve, to argue for something that sounds morbid and isn’t: deliberately and regularly confronting your own mortality, rather than pushing the thought away, is what cuts through the petty distractions and manufactured urgency most people spend their lives on. He calls the resulting feeling — the sense of being briefly, improbably alive inside something far larger than yourself — the Sublime, and argues it’s accessible through smaller doses too: a night sky, a vast landscape, genuine contemplation of how unlikely your own existence was.

Share this: Once a week, actually sit with the fact that you will die, specifically and without euphemism, instead of deflecting the thought the way you probably do by instinct. People who do this report it doesn’t produce despair — it produces urgency about what actually matters and indifference toward what doesn’t.

Conclusion

Almost none of the conflict in your life is caused by other people’s stated reasons for what they do. It’s caused by the emotions, patterns, and repressed Shadow underneath those reasons — in them, and in you.

A short checklist to carry out of this one:

  • Before a big decision, ask whether you’re currently calm enough to trust your own reasoning — if not, wait.
  • When evaluating someone important, pull up their actual track record instead of their pitch.
  • Notice the split-second crack in someone’s composure; it tells you more than their words do.
  • Name your envy out loud to yourself the moment you feel it, rather than relabeling it as something more flattering.
  • Before adopting a group’s intensity about something, check whether you’d hold that position alone.
  • Once a week, sit with your own mortality on purpose instead of pushing the thought away.

One honest caveat: Greene writes almost entirely through historical anecdote rather than citation-heavy research, and he’s working from psychoanalytic frameworks — Jung’s Shadow, repression — that have fallen out of favor in mainstream academic psychology even where the underlying observations still ring true. Treat the stories as illustrations of real patterns, not as proof in the scientific sense.

Source: The Laws of Human Nature by Robert Greene, 2018.

item.title: Be the Worst Person in the Room: Career Lessons From a Jazz Saxophonist Turned Programmer
item.description: Seven career ideas from Chad Fowler's The Passionate Programmer, from why you should be the weakest player in the band to why your career is a project you can't plan up front.
item.content:encoded:
Here is career advice that sounds like sabotage: be the worst person in the room.

Chad Fowler was a professional jazz and blues saxophonist before he moved into software, and he built a whole book on lessons like that one. The Passionate Programmer is written for people who code, but nearly every idea works for anyone whose skills can go stale. These are the seven I’d keep.

1. Be the worst person in the room

Your skills drift toward the level of the people around you, so choose them on purpose.

Fowler picked up a rule from jazz guitarist Pat Metheny: “Always be the worst guy in every band you’re in.” Standing next to musicians he admired, he was sure he’d be thrown off the bandstand. Instead, his playing started to match theirs, the way you pick up an accent after a few weeks abroad. The reverse also held. In weak bar bands he played like those bands, and the bad habits followed him to better gigs.

There was a second surprise. He wasn’t as bad as he feared, and he had proof: good musicians only call you back if they want to play with you again, and they kept calling. Aiming for the bottom stopped him from selling himself short.

Share this: if you can’t switch teams, join an open-source project you admire or a local developer meetup, and spend time with people a level above you.

2. Practice should sound ugly

Practicing and performing are different jobs, and most of us only do the second.

Fowler remembers the music-school practice rooms: ugly sounds through thin walls, from players who were very good. Practice is supposed to sound bad because you’re working at the edge of your ability. Athletes do their straining behind closed doors, too. Software, he argues, is the odd profession where people practice on the job, in public, on the employer’s time.

His fix was to write software nobody needed, so there was no pressure to cut corners. The results were awkward, and he came to read the awkwardness as a good sign. If only elegant code comes out of a practice session, you’re sitting near the center of what you can already do.

Share this: pick one dusty corner of your main tool (he suggests regular expressions, a compact way to describe text patterns) and drill it on a throwaway project. Then read other people’s code the way a studio musician sight-reads a new score.

3. Treat your skills like an investment portfolio

Every skill you learn is a bet, and bets have risk and reward.

Fowler runs a thought experiment about three technologies. Learning COBOL, an old business language, was safe: work was easy to find, but it didn’t pay spectacularly. Learning Java early was risky, since few employers used it at first, but it could pay very well for those who got in early. Learning BeOS, a dazzling new operating system, was risky and paid nothing: it never caught on, and the developers who mastered it never got their investment back.

Then he adds a twist. Old systems don’t die, they get replaced in stages, and during the handover the old and new have to talk to each other. Young developers don’t know the old systems and veterans don’t know the new ones. That gap is a job he calls technology hospice: be the person still able to support critical systems after everyone else has moved on, and you hold the leverage. The risk is real, because one day you’ll be an expert in something that no longer exists. His answer is to move fast and find the next fading system.

Share this: draw a line on paper, newest tools on the left and sunsetting ones on the right. Mark where your skills sit. If they clump in one spot, that’s your exposure.

4. You can’t win on price, so build robots

If you compete on hourly cost, someone cheaper will always appear.

Fowler tells the story of early web design. When websites were new, companies paid thousands of dollars for a basic one, and he gives 5,000astheexample.Peoplenoticed,learnedHTML,andthemarketflooded.Soonthesamecompanieswouldpay5,000 as the example. People noticed, learned HTML, and the market flooded. Soon the same companies would pay 5,000astheexample.Peoplenoticed,learnedHTML,andthemarketflooded.Soonthesamecompanieswouldpay500. Offshore programming, he argues, injected a large supply of low-cost labor, and you can’t afford to fight on price.

Managers can’t easily measure how fast a programmer is, so they count what they can: cost per hour. That leaves three ways to produce more software: faster people, more people, or automation. Faster is hard to prove, and he doesn’t want to encourage the cheap-army approach. Automation is the one left. He points to the factory robots of the 1980s: everyone was upset except the people who built the robots.

Share this: pick one task you repeat, and write a small program that does it for you. Start simple and don’t worry about reuse.

5. The boring job may be the freest one

Low expectations are a kind of freedom.

When Fowler helped set up a 250-person development center from scratch, he hit a surprise. Everyone wanted to build new systems and nobody wanted to maintain old ones. Maintenance looked low-status and messy, and new projects looked like the road to promotion.

His coffee analogy flips it. Give someone $1,000 and ask for a coffee, and you’ll be furious if they return with neither money nor coffee. Give them nothing and ask for a coffee, and you’ll be grateful if it shows up and understanding if it doesn’t. Project work is the first case: well funded, closely watched, expected to deliver. Maintenance is the second: nobody expects anything flashy, customers stay hands-off, and a bug that forces a redesign of part of the system is just part of fixing bugs. For a creative person, that can be the more open playground.

Share this: next time you want to dodge the unglamorous task, ask what you could do with it precisely because nobody is watching.

6. Work like you only have eight hours

Scarce time gets used better than plentiful time.

The Extreme Programming movement, a style of software teamwork, says people should work no more than forty hours a week. That upset managers and many programmers too, for whom long hours were a badge of toughness. Bob Martin, a well-known voice in that movement, renamed the idea the eight-hour burn: work so relentlessly that you couldn’t possibly continue past eight hours.

Fowler’s argument has two parts. Tired people make mistakes that cost time and money, and projects are marathons, not sprints. And your hours behave like money: when you have seventy to spend, each one feels cheap. By day four of a seventy-hour week, it’s 10:30 a.m., you know you’ll be there long after everyone else leaves, and you start reading tech news. A hard stop makes you rank your tasks and attack them one at a time.

Share this: set a firm finish time tomorrow, list your tasks in priority order before you start, and see how much of the list is done when the clock hits it.

7. Don’t plan your career like a waterfall project

You can’t know up front what you’ll want, so a ten-year blueprint will fail for the same reason big software plans do.

In the old way of building software, called waterfall, analysts write huge specifications, architects hand down designs, and after months or years the result arrives, thoroughly tested and not what anyone wanted. A group of developers rebelled and created the agile family of methods, built around the assumption that change is constant. Fowler later realized he had planned his own career like a waterfall project: newbie programmer, architect, manager, director, on track to become a vice president or chief information officer. The more he succeeded, the less he liked the work. He was efficiently building a career he didn’t want.

The fix was to change it, and for him that meant returning to hands-on technology. He pairs this with a warning about value rigidity: beliefs you hold so firmly you never test them. Like a frog in slowly heating water, you don’t notice the change. Many network administrators in the mid-1990s swore by Novell’s NetWare. No single event ended it, and by the time they noticed, the water was boiling.

Share this: make two columns, career and technology, and list the beliefs you never question. Then ask which ones you would drop if the evidence changed.

Conclusion

Your career is the biggest project you will ever run, so run it like a good team runs software: get feedback from people better than you, practice at your limits, automate the repetitive parts, and change course the moment the plan stops fitting.

  • Spend this month somewhere you’re the weakest player.
  • Schedule one practice session that is allowed to sound bad.
  • Map your skills on the new-to-sunsetting line.
  • Automate one task you repeat every week.
  • Write down one career belief you’ve never questioned, and challenge it.

One caveat

This is a book of experience and opinion, not research. Fowler backs most points with stories from his own career, and the eight-hour burn and be-the-worst ideas rest on his reasoning, not on studies. His examples also come from 2009. The technologies he names, such as J2EE and .NET, and his worries about offshore competition belong to that moment, and technology hospice is a gamble he admits himself. Keep the habits and treat the specifics as dated.

Source: Chad Fowler, The Passionate Programmer: Creating a Remarkable Career in Software Development (2009).

item.title: Stop Trying to Be Original: 7 Ways to Steal Like an Artist (Without Being a Thief)
item.description: Seven ideas from Austin Kleon's Steal Like an Artist on copying your heroes, making what you wish existed, and getting more done by being boring.
item.content:encoded:
Every artist gets asked where their ideas come from, and Austin Kleon says the honest answer is three words: “I steal them.”

That sounds like a confession, but it works better as a method. In Steal Like an Artist, Kleon argues that nothing comes from nowhere, and that the people who look most original are usually the ones who borrowed from the most places. It’s a short book for anyone who makes things, whether that’s songs, spreadsheets or sales pitches.

Here are the seven ideas I’d pass on.

1. Nothing is original, so become a curator

Every new idea is a remix of older ones, which makes your taste your main tool.

Kleon borrows an art-school trick. Draw two parallel lines and ask how many lines you see. There are two, plus the empty space between them: 1 + 1 = 3. Ideas combine the same way, and so do you. You’re a mashup of the teachers, music and books you chose to let in. Writer Jonathan Lethem, he notes, says that when people call something original, nine times out of ten they simply don’t know the sources.

The difference between a collector and a hoarder is selectivity. Hoarders keep everything, artists keep what they love. And don’t try to swallow your whole field at once. Study one thinker you love, learn everything about them, then study three people they loved, and keep climbing. Once you’ve built your tree, grow your own branch.

Share this: start a swipe file, a folder or scrapbook of things worth stealing, and write down the first hero for your tree.

2. Copy the thinking, not the surface

Copying is how everyone learns, so aim at how your heroes see, not how their work looks.

Writers copy the alphabet, musicians play scales, painters reproduce masterpieces. The Beatles started as a cover band, and Paul McCartney says they began writing their own songs partly to stop other bands from playing their set. Kleon’s rule is to copy many heroes, not one. Copy one author and it’s plagiarism, goes the line he quotes, but copy many and it’s research.

The best part comes when you fail. Kobe Bryant stole his moves from tapes of players he admired, but his body couldn’t pull them off the same way, so he adapted them. Kleon retells Conan O’Brien’s version of the pattern: Johnny Carson tried to be Jack Benny and became Carson, David Letterman tried to be Carson and became Letterman, and O’Brien tried to be Letterman and became O’Brien. Our inability to make perfect copies is where our own voice hides.

Share this: copy a hero’s work closely, note exactly where your version falls short, then amplify those differences.

3. Write the book you want to read

Instead of making what you know, make what you wish already existed.

Kleon’s example is humbling. Jurassic Park came out on his tenth birthday, and the next day he typed up his own sequel on the family computer. He didn’t know it, but he was writing fan fiction. The real sequel arrived years later and disappointed him, because it never matches the one in your head.

That’s his point. Advice to write what you know tends to produce stories where nothing happens. Write what you like instead. Musician Bradford Cox, as a kid, recorded fake versions of his favorite band’s upcoming albums, then compared them with the real ones. Many of those songs eventually became songs for his own band, Deerhunter.

Share this: think of your favorite creators and ask what they missed, then go make that.

4. Start before you know who you are

You don’t find yourself first and then make things. You find yourself by making things.

Kleon says that if he’d waited to understand who he was, he’d still be sitting around figuring it out. He’s blunt about impostor syndrome, the feeling of being a phony who’s winging it: nobody doing real creative work knows where the good stuff comes from. They show up and do the work every day. His take on the old fake-it-until-you-make-it line has two readings, and he likes both. Act like the person you want to be, and keep pretending to make something until you actually do.

He also finds freedom in being unknown. When nobody’s watching, there’s no image to manage and no paycheck on the line, so you can experiment and get better. Once attention and money arrive, you never get that back. His advice is to enjoy your obscurity while it lasts, and use it.

Share this: make the first ugly version this week, and don’t announce it.

5. Put your hands back in your work

The computer is good for editing and publishing, but bad at generating ideas.

Kleon says it’s too easy to hit delete, so the computer turns us into perfectionists who edit ideas before we’ve had them. Cartoonist Tom Gauld, he reports, stays off the computer until most of his thinking is done, because once it’s involved, everything is on a path to being finished.

Kleon’s own setup is two desks. The analog desk holds markers, pens, pencils, paper, index cards and newspaper, and nothing electronic is allowed. The digital desk has the laptop, scanner and drawing tablet. His first book, Newspaper Blackout, was made hands first, then computer, then hands, then computer. Every poem was made from a newspaper article and a permanent marker.

Share this: spend about $10 on paper, pens and sticky notes, and set up an analog corner. Stand up, pin things on the wall, and move to the screen only once you have something to execute.

6. Be boring so your work can be wild

Creative energy is finite, so protect it with a dull, steady life.

Kleon calls himself a boring guy with a nine-to-five job. The image of the genius burning out young, he says, is for superhumans and people who want to die young. His version: eat breakfast, sleep, go for long walks. Even Patti Smith, he says, tells young artists to go to the dentist.

He’s a fan of the day job, too. It pays the bills, puts you around other people to learn from, and gives you a routine. Money worries cost you freedom in your art, so he recommends a budget, packing your lunch, and holding on to what you earn. For the work itself, he leans on Jerry Seinfeld’s method: hang a wall calendar showing the whole year and put a big X on each day you do the work. Soon you have a chain, and your only job is not to break it.

Share this: buy a calendar tonight, pick one daily task, and start the chain.

7. Creativity is subtraction

Limits don’t kill creativity, they cure creative block.

Kleon says the idea that you can do anything is terrifying, and that endless possibility paralyzes. The cure is to add constraints: write a song on your lunch break, paint with one color, start a business with no start-up capital. His favorite example is Dr. Seuss, who wrote The Cat in the Hat using only 236 different words. His editor then bet he couldn’t write a book with just 50, and Seuss won the bet with Green Eggs and Ham.

This also closes the loop with the first idea. If you’re a mashup of what you let in, you’re equally defined by what you leave out. Curating influences is subtraction, and so is choosing what not to copy and what not to put in your work.

Share this: add one constraint to your next project, such as less time, fewer materials or fewer words.

Conclusion

You’re not original because you invent from nothing. You’re original because of what you choose to take in, what you choose to copy, and what you choose to leave out.

  • Start a swipe file this week.
  • Pick one hero and copy their thinking, not just their style.
  • Make the thing you wish existed.
  • Do your first draft on paper.
  • Mark a calendar every day you work.
  • Add one constraint to your next project.

One caveat

This is a short, opinionated book built on the author’s own experience and a lot of borrowed quotes, not on research. It dates from 2012, and its advice on sharing, which boils down to putting your work on the Internet, is far less of a guarantee of being seen today. Kleon also separates copying to learn from passing off someone’s work as yours, but he doesn’t give you a test for where homage ends and theft begins. You have to draw that line yourself. He admits as much: take what you can use and leave the rest.

Source: Austin Kleon, Steal Like an Artist: 10 Things Nobody Told You About Being Creative (2012).

item.title: Your Gut Feeling Is a Con Artist (and You're the Mark)
item.description: Seven ideas stolen from Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow that will make you trust your own confidence a lot less, and decide a lot better.
item.content:encoded:
Here is the most unsettling sentence I took from a 500-page book:

How sure you feel tells you almost nothing about whether you’re right.

It tells you something else: how smoothly your brain managed to assemble a story. That’s it. Smooth story, high confidence. Messy story, doubt. Truth is not part of the calculation.

That’s the thread running through Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow, the life’s work of a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. I read it so you don’t have to, and kept only the ideas worth sharing. Here are the seven that survived.

1. What you see is all there is

Your fast, automatic mind (Kahneman calls it System 1) works with whatever information happens to be lying around, builds the best story it can from it, and hands you the result with a feeling of certainty.

It never says “I’m missing something.” Information it doesn’t have simply doesn’t exist for it. Kahneman’s abbreviation for this is WYSIATI: what you see is all there is.

The experiment that made me wince: people read a legal case, then heard from a lawyer for one side only. They were told they were hearing one side. They could have easily imagined the other lawyer’s pitch. Still, they were more confident in their verdicts than people who heard both sides.

Less information, more confidence. A thin story is easier to make coherent than a rich one.

Share this: when you feel certain, ask “what would I need to know that I don’t know?” Then go find it before you decide.

2. You rarely answer the question you were asked

When a question is hard, your mind quietly swaps it for an easier one and answers that, without telling you.

  • How happy are you with your life? becomes What’s my mood right now?
  • Will this candidate be a good leader? becomes Does she look like a leader?
  • How popular will the president be in six months? becomes How popular is the president today?

You don’t feel the swap. The answer arrives fast and fluent, so it feels like an answer to the real question.

Share this: for any big judgment, write the actual question down. Then ask: “Is this really what I’m answering?”

3. Confidence is a feeling, not evidence

Early in his career, Kahneman helped evaluate soldiers for officer training in the Israeli army. He and his colleagues watched candidates tackle an obstacle course and felt they could see each man’s true character. Then every few months they’d get feedback: their predictions were barely better than guessing.

It changed nothing. The next batch arrived, they watched them haul a log over a wall, and the certainty came right back, as vivid as before.

He named it the illusion of validity: you can know, as a statistic, that your judgments are poor, and still feel that this specific judgment is solid. Like the Müller-Lyer lines, knowing the trick doesn’t make it go away.

Share this: high confidence from someone (including you) mostly proves they’ve told themselves a coherent story. Treat admitted uncertainty as the more informative signal.

4. A dumb formula beats the smart expert

Paul Meehl dared to compare trained clinicians against simple statistical rules. The rules won, and kept winning. After roughly 200 studies, about 60% show the algorithm clearly more accurate, and the rest are ties. Predicting parole violations, business success, cancer survival, college grades. Kahneman notes that no exception has been convincingly documented.

Why do experts lose?

  • They try to be clever and combine many factors, and complexity usually hurts.
  • They are wildly inconsistent. Experienced radiologists contradict their own reading of the same X-ray about 20% of the time.

An economist built a three-variable weather formula that predicts the future price of Bordeaux wine better than the tasters do. And the best-known success story of all is the Apgar score: five quick checks, scored 0 to 2, that replaced gut feel in delivery rooms and, in Kahneman’s telling, has saved the lives of hundreds of thousands of infants.

Even a back-of-the-envelope formula with equal weights often competes with fancy statistics. One of Kahneman’s favorite examples: predict a marriage with how often you make love minus how often you quarrel.

Share this: for hiring, investing, prioritizing, anything repeated, pick 4 to 6 relevant criteria, score each one separately, add them up, and let the total decide. Use your gut to collect the scores, not to overrule the sum.

5. The test for when to trust intuition

Kahneman isn’t saying all intuition is garbage. He spent years arguing with Gary Klein, who studied firefighters that sensed a floor was about to collapse. They finally agreed on a two-part test. Trust an expert’s gut only if:

  1. The environment is regular enough to be predictable, and
  2. They’ve had long practice with fast, clear feedback.

Chess players, nurses, firefighters, anesthesiologists pass. Stock pickers and long-range political pundits fail, because their world offers no stable patterns to learn. Some environments are worse than useless: Kahneman retells the story of a doctor who “predicted” typhoid in patients. He was accurate, because he was spreading it himself with unwashed hands.

And the line I keep repeating to myself: don’t trust anyone, yourself included, to tell you how much to trust their judgment. Judge the environment and the feedback loop, not the confidence.

Share this: before you defer to an expert (or to your own hunch), ask two questions. Is this a world with stable patterns? Did this person get quick, honest feedback in it?

6. Your plan is a best-case fantasy, so imagine the funeral first

Plans are written from the inside: our team, our scenario, our enthusiasm. Kahneman calls the result the planning fallacy, forecasts hugging the best case instead of the track record of similar projects.

The receipts:

  • Scotland’s new parliament building: estimated at up to £40 million, finished at around £431 million.
  • Rail projects worldwide: ridership overestimated by 106% on average, costs overrun by 45%.
  • Home kitchen remodels: owners expected to pay about 18,658andpaidabout18,658 and paid about 18,658andpaidabout38,769.

Two fixes:

  • The outside view. Ignore your story. Look up how similar projects actually went, and start your estimate there.
  • The premortem (Klein’s idea). Before committing, gather the team and say: “Imagine it’s a year from now. We did this. It was a disaster. Write the history of why.” It works because it makes doubt socially safe. Once a group has decided, dissent starts to look like disloyalty. The premortem makes dissent the assignment.

Share this: run a ten-minute premortem on your next big decision. Then multiply your timeline by whatever similar projects actually took.

7. You’re two people, and the wrong one is running your life

Kahneman splits you into an experiencing self (the one who feels each moment) and a remembering self (the one who keeps score afterward). They disagree, and the remembering self gets the vote.

In a colonoscopy study, patients reported their pain minute by minute. Afterward, they rated the whole ordeal, and their ratings ignored how long it lasted. What mattered was the worst moment and the final moment: the peak-end rule, plus duration neglect. A patient with an 8-minute procedure that ended painfully remembered it as worse than a patient whose procedure was three times longer but tapered off gently.

The same distortion shapes how we judge our lives. Kahneman’s focusing illusion: whatever you’re thinking about seems far more important than it really is. People assume sunny California must make you happier. It doesn’t, because Californians hardly think about the weather. The same trap makes us overestimate how much a new car, house, or gadget will improve our daily lives, and underrate things like friendships and hobbies that keep demanding our attention.

Share this: end experiences well, because the ending is what gets remembered. And before a big purchase or move, ask: “How often will I actually be thinking about this?”

Conclusion

If you only keep one thing:

Your mind is a story machine. It values coherence over completeness, ease over accuracy, and confidence over evidence.

You can’t switch that machine off, and Kahneman is clear that even he never fully escaped its tricks. But you can build around it:

  • Look for what’s missing.
  • Name the real question.
  • Distrust the feeling of certainty.
  • Let simple formulas make the repeated calls.
  • Check whether the environment lets anyone have real expertise.
  • Run the premortem.
  • Plan for the memory, and for the attention, not just the moment.

The goal isn’t to stop having a gut. It’s to stop letting your gut cross-examine itself and rule that it’s innocent.

One honest caveat: some findings in the book, especially around social priming, have not held up well in replication, and I left those out on purpose. The ideas above rest on far firmer ground.

Source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).
